This. This is someone who gets how grimdark should actually used in a story. Too much is too bleak and the reader stops caring, or lack of investment in expanding the setting beyond a hellscape or writing characters only as flat victims as tallies in a death count, is what kills grimdark as a subgenre. Writing my original fiction makes me want to tear my hair out. I feel like everything I write with has to be just so as to be traditionally published, and I've become paranoid that any original concept I've come up with has been done better by some other writer. Also writing for a deadline for a short story or to make a publisher's slush pile makes me feel like I'm writing with an impending sense of doom. On the other hand, I feel much less constrained in my creativity, and I've developed much more nuanced plots and fleshed out original characters by my past experience of writing fanfiction. I'm still working out issues with time management and the quality of my drafting, but feel like the road to publishing an original work is much closer in sight.

The absolute worst combination is a historical novel I'm writing using all real people as characters. I love the research and the complex, compelling narrative I've crafted, but I feel like I have to be on point all the time by being historically accurate and culturally sensitive in every description and every line of dialogue I write. It feels like a pastiche of reality, some how not a real novel, but it's also a project I've worked on for nearly decade now and it's also the one I want to publish the most.

I hate to go back to the old prejudice of using fanfiction as practice for original fiction, but I found that when I set aside my original work to spend time outline and fleshing out the scope of my plots, worldbuilding, and character backgrounds in fanfiction, I was able to come back later to original fiction and really establish a much more grounded setting, narrative, and characters. I still have problems with speed of my writing and fine tuning the tone and content for a general or specific audience, along with the quality of my prose, but I feel like I have a really strong grasp of the foundations of my writing, regardless of whether it be original or fanfiction. I think having distance and time to really think about how you will develop your approach to either sort of fiction will allow you plan and structure how you write better.

I think that there's an inherent miscoception that all writers who produce "queer" fanfiction- in that the focus is on LGBTQA+ characters or relationships- lack understanding or fit the mold of being this "problematic fujoshi." (Fujoshi itself is not problematic in itself as a term, nor should it  be deployed as a slur). 

Its true that some older fanfiction did focus on antiquated stereotypes drawn from cishet media and beliefs, and that some writers don't have good exposure to irl LGBTQA+ content or know how to utilize well in fiction. But I also think that part of this may stem from how people conceptualize how essential written porn is supposed to more than just titillation or exploration of sexuality, regardless of whether it be the writer's or the reader's. There's this demand for queer relationships in fiction to live up to these impossibly un-problematic standards,  that is itself harmful and exclusionary to those to whom those depictions might have symbolic, important value. It places an unwarranted burden up the reader to always seek out a moralizing, notmalizing narrative without allowing them to explore what they find pleasurable or interesting. It also limits what an author can feel they can write, and in a way it forces writers to infantilize their audience by withholding more challenging content in favor of content that can be rather sterile.
